slides.subtitle: Teach what you found

mascot.say: Hi, I'm Mi. Let's notice, test and explain why!

slides.title: I remember: a pattern

blocks.text: Count in 3s. What are the next two numbers?

slides.note: A pattern (Term 1 Lesson 4 and Term 2 Lesson 6, taught again with a picture). The numbers go 3, 6, 9, 12 and then two empty boxes. Ask: what are the next two numbers (15 and 18). Then ask for volunteers: who remembers a pattern from this year? A pass is always fine. A child who is unsure counts on fingers, three at a time. Your turn, no new picture: count in 3s from 18 (21, 24). Children answer aloud. No writing.

slides.title: I remember: a way to add

blocks.text: Make a ten first. What is 8 + 6?

slides.note: A way to add (Term 1 Lesson 5, taught again on a number line). 8 and 2 make 10, then 4 more makes 14: the 6 was split into 2 and 4. Ask: what is 8 + 6 (14). A child who is unsure counts on from 8 on fingers, six times. Your turn, no new picture: 9 + 5 (9 and 1 make 10, then 4 more is 14). Children answer aloud. No writing.

slides.note: Puzzle 1 is an access question: Ali has 6 pens and Mei has 4 pens, and the child writes a question (how many pens in all, how many more pens does Ali have than Mei: many questions are right). slides.title: Explore: which puzzle is good?

rows: Ali has 8 pens and Mei has 5 pens.
Think of an even number between 1 and 20.
Ravi has 7 pencils. Jamie has 2 more pencils than Ravi. How many pencils does Jamie have?

blocks.text: Which puzzle is a good puzzle? What is wrong with the others?

slides.note: Round 1, about 3 minutes. Read the three puzzles aloud with their numbers, then ask: which one is a good puzzle, and what is wrong with the others. Take answers from volunteers; a pass is fine. Answers are on the next slide: A has no question; B has many answers (2, 4, 6 and so on); C is a good puzzle. A child who says C because it is longer: ask, what does C have that A and B do not? Nobody holds paper to the camera.

slides.title: A good puzzle

blocks.text: A has no question. B has many answers. C is good: a story, numbers, one question and one answer.

slides.note: The answer for round 1. Puzzle A has numbers but no question. Puzzle B has no single answer: any even number from 2 to 18 fits. Puzzle C has a story, numbers and one question, and exactly one answer (9). Say: a good puzzle has a story, numbers, one question and one answer. Children tick their own thinking with a tick. Do not name any child.

slides.title: Explore: write your own puzzle

items: Pick two numbers up to 20.
Write a short story with a name.
Write one question.
Solve it.
Check it a second way.

blocks.text: Use your own paper. Then tell your quest partner your puzzle.

slides.note: Round 2, about 5 minutes. Read the five steps one at a time. Children write their own puzzle on their own paper: two numbers up to 20, a short story with a name, one question. They solve it, then check it a second way (a different method or working backwards). The quest partner may solve it quietly. Walk the cameras and ask how do you know. A child who needs help starts with two numbers and a name: Mei has 6 and Ben has 3. A child who writes a puzzle with two answers: ask, how many answers does it have? Puzzles stay inside the group: nobody shares a puzzle outside the group unless the grown-up agrees. Nobody holds paper to the camera.

slides.title: What did we notice?

items: What does a good puzzle need?
Why do we check a puzzle a second way?

slides.note: Take one or two answers from volunteers. Key ideas: a story, numbers, one question and one answer; a second check can find a puzzle with two answers or a wrong answer; a hard puzzle is not better than a clear one. Repeat each child answer in your own words so the recording picks it up. Do not give the rule before the children say it; the mini-lesson makes it exact.

slides.title: Teach it in one minute

blocks.head: MY IDEA
items: My favourite idea is counting by rows.
It works like this: count one row, then count on by rows.
Here is an example: 3 rows of 4 squares. 4, 8, 12.
Check: 3 rows of 4 is 4 + 4 + 4 = 12.

slides.note: Modelled teaching, about 90 seconds. The frame has four lines: my favourite idea is; it works like this; here is an example; check. Read the model aloud, pointing to the rows of the grid: 4, 8, 12. Say: you will use these four lines in the Showcase; you may use your favourite page to help you. A pass is always fine and you may teach your grown-up instead. Say: your voice is recorded if you are not muted. Do not say best or better about any idea.

slides.title: A puzzle with a rule

blocks.head: MI'S PUZZLE
items: Two numbers add up to 9.
One number is 3 more than the other.
What are the two numbers?

blocks.text: List every pair that makes 9. Then find the pair that fits.

slides.note: Worked example, a puzzle with a rule. Children list every pair of whole numbers that make 9 on their own paper, starting with 0 and 9, and find the pair whose difference is 3. Ask: what are the two numbers (3 and 6). The answer is on the next slide. Say: listing every pair shows that no other pair works. That is a proof. A child who writes 6 and 3 and stops has the answer: ask, how do you know there is not another pair?

slides.title: Only one pair fits

blocks.text: Only 3 and 6 differ by 3. The answer is 3 and 6, and no other pair works.

slides.note: The answer for the example on the slide before. The five pairs are 0 and 9, 1 and 8, 2 and 7, 3 and 6, 4 and 5; the differences are 9, 7, 5, 3 and 1. Only 3 and 6 differ by 3. Read it aloud so that children can tick their own work. Say: we listed every case, so the answer must be right and it is the only answer.

slides.title: Check a friend's puzzle

blocks.head: A CHILD IN ANOTHER CLASS WROTE
items: Two numbers add up to 8.
One number is 2 more than the other.
The numbers are 6 and 2.

blocks.text: Is the puzzle right? How do you know?

slides.note: Worked example, checking. Children check both clues on their own paper: 6 and 2 add up to 8 (the first clue fits), but 6 is 4 more than 2, not 2 more (the second clue does not). Ask: is the puzzle right (no); how do you know. The answer is on the next slide. Say: check every clue, not just one. The child in the story is in another class: no cast name is given the wrong answer.

slides.title: The second clue does not fit

blocks.text: No. 6 + 2 = 8, but 6 is 4 more than 2, not 2 more. The numbers that fit are 5 and 3.

slides.note: The answer for the example on the slide before. The first clue fits: 6 and 2 make 8. The second clue does not: 6 take away 2 is 4, not 2. The right numbers are 5 and 3: 5 + 3 = 8 and 5 take away 3 is 2. Read it aloud so that children can tick their own work. Say: a friend's puzzle is checked clue by clue.

slides.title: Before you share a puzzle

items: It has a story, numbers and one question.
It has exactly one answer.
You checked it a second way.
It is your own puzzle: not copied.

slides.note: Read the four checks aloud. Say: these are the four checks for the puzzle in the workbook and for the Showcase. Say: a puzzle is shared inside our group only, unless your grown-up says yes. Take one answer to: which check would you do first. Do not collect puzzles and do not compile them. About 1 minute.

slides.title: A year in moves

blocks.text: Stand up. Make a quarter turn.
Count in 3s and clap each time.
Sip some water.

slides.note: Four minutes. Stand up on camera with a little clear space. Make a slow quarter turn (the same as a quarter of a circle) and sit or stand still again. Count in 3s from 0 to 18 with a clap each time. Stretch up high, then curl small, like a shape being folded in half. Ask: how many claps to reach 18 (6). No equipment, no running. A child may stay seated and move one arm. Do not give prizes or compare children.

slides.title: Showcase

blocks.head: TEACH US IN ABOUT A MINUTE
items: My favourite idea is ___.
My tool is ___ because ___.

blocks.text: Volunteers only. A pass is always fine.

slides.note: The Showcase, about 11 minutes. Volunteers teach one favourite idea from the year in about a minute with the frame on the slide (the idea, the tool and why, an example and a check); they may hold a page up to themselves, not to the camera, and may read from their page. Rules, said aloud before anyone starts: a pass is always fine; you may teach your grown-up instead (microphone muted) and tell us I taught my grown-up; your voice is recorded if you are not muted; everyone else listens, and afterwards may say one thing they learned; no voting, no best, no ranking, no counting of claps. Take up to five volunteers, one at a time, volunteers first; repeat each idea in your own words so the recording picks it up. Puzzles are shared inside the group only. Nobody collects a puzzle.

slides.note: Two minutes. Children pick one problem from today and fill in the look-back box on page 5: three questions, the Tool I used row, and the stuck and pass boxes. A pass is always allowed. If a child ticks I am still stuck, a grown-up may photograph that page and send it to the business WhatsApp (the number is in the parent summary, never on a slide); you then help in the open session when the next program starts. lines.text: Greet the whole group warmly, before the recording starts. Check that you can see each child, or ask the grown-up.
Hello, inquirers! Pencil ready, and your workbook. Cameras can be on or off, as you like.
This lesson is recorded so a friend who is away can catch up. The recording has me, the shared screen and any voice that is not muted. You may keep your microphone and camera off.
Start the recording now. Do not use children's first names on the recording.
@rec
Microphone off until I ask you to speak. To answer, say it with me on three, show fingers, or give a thumbs up. Nobody holds paper up to the camera.
Today is the last lesson of the year. We teach one idea we found, we write a puzzle, and we play Mi's Challenge Quest.
Today you choose the tool.
Point at the row of tools on page 1 of the workbook.

Say the recording statement and the microphone routine in the same words every lesson, for anyone who joined late. Say the notice before you start the recording, and do not use children's first names once it is running. The routine and the four inquirer rules were introduced earlier in the year: do not re-teach them.

Plain statement for families when it comes up: writing a puzzle with a rule and showing why its answer must be right goes beyond Primary 1 on purpose, at Think harder and Go further only; the Quest gate on picture graphs reads a key where each picture stands for 2, which is Primary 2.

New here? Say in one minute: our three rule words (notice it, test it, explain why); a guess is fine and you can always pass; after Start here you may try Think harder, Go further or the Investigation at home; nobody holds paper to the camera. Nothing from earlier lessons is needed.
@rec
Three things we remember from the year. First, a pattern. Count in threes.
What are the next two numbers? Who remembers a pattern from this year? A pass is always fine.
Your turn. Count in threes from eighteen. Say it with me.
Second, a way to add. We make a ten first.
What is eight and six? Count on with your fingers.
Your turn. What is nine and five? Say it with me.
Third, our eight tools. Draw it, act it out, spot the pattern, list every way, make a table, work backwards, guess and check, and try something simpler.
Which tool have you used the most this year? Say it, or point to it on your Toolbox Card.
Your turn. Pick one tool and say one problem it could help with. Say it with me.
Say each answer with me: fifteen and eighteen; fourteen; eight; twenty-one and twenty-four; fourteen; twelve. Then stretch your fingers.
If a child is unsure about the pattern, count on fingers three at a time. For making a ten, count on from eight six times. For the tools, read each row slowly and let the child point to a card.

Answers: the next numbers are 15 and 18; 8 and 6 make 14; any tool with a reason. Your turns: 21 and 24; 14. Children answer with a whisper, fingers or hands. Nobody writes. Joining cold: the toolbox page is all you need.
@rec
Two sneak-peek puzzles: ideas we have not learnt yet. A guess is a great start, and I do not know is welcome. Your paper is not collected.
Puzzle one. Ali has six pens. Mei has four pens. Write a question for this puzzle.
Children write on their own paper.
Puzzle two. Write a number bigger than three and smaller than eight. Is this a good puzzle? Circle Yes or No. I know because blank.
Children write or draw their answer.
Keep your paper. Nobody shows it. We will check our own thinking later, at the Showcase.

Puzzle 1 answer: many questions are right (how many pens in all, how many more pens does Ali have than Mei). Puzzle 2 answer: No, because 4, 5, 6 and 7 all fit. A child who writes 5 has answered it: do not correct it now. Look for good ideas to praise later. Do not write scores or keep a list.
@rec
Today we are puzzle makers. Three puzzles first. Listen.

Puzzle A. Ali has eight pens and Mei has five pens. Puzzle B. Think of an even number between one and twenty. Puzzle C. Ravi has seven pencils. Jamie has two more pencils than Ravi. How many pencils does Jamie have?
Which puzzle is a good puzzle? What is wrong with the others? A pass is always fine.
A has no question. B has many answers. C is a good puzzle: a story, numbers, one question and one answer.
Now you write your own puzzle on your own paper. Read the five steps with me.
One. Pick two numbers up to twenty. Two. Write a short story with a name. Three. Write one question. Four. Solve it. Five. Check it a second way.
Children write, solve and check their own puzzle. Tutor walks the cameras and asks how do you know. Quest partners may solve it quietly.
What does a good puzzle need? Why do we check a puzzle a second way?
A good puzzle has a story, numbers, one question and one answer. A second check can find a mistake.

A child who needs help starts with two numbers and a name: Mei has six and Ben has three. A child whose puzzle has two answers: ask, how many answers does it have? A child who cannot check a second way: work backwards, or draw it.

Main room only. Puzzle answers: A has no question; B has many answers; C is good (9). Puzzles stay inside the group: nobody shares a puzzle outside the group unless the grown-up agrees. Do not say the rule before the children do.
@rec
Teach it in one minute. I teach you an idea I like, in four lines.

My favourite idea is counting by rows. It works like this: count one row, then count on by rows. Here is an example: three rows of four squares. Four, eight, twelve. Check: three rows of four is four and four and four, twelve.
You will use the same four lines in the Showcase. Your voice is recorded if you are not muted. A pass is always fine, and you may teach your grown-up instead.
Rehearse: children say the four lines for their own favourite idea to their quest partner, in a whisper. Tutor walks the cameras.
A puzzle with a rule. Mi's puzzle. Two numbers add up to nine. One number is three more than the other.
What are the two numbers? List every pair that makes nine on your paper.
Nought and nine. One and eight. Two and seven. Three and six. Four and five. Only three and six are three apart. The answer is three and six, and no other pair works. Listing every case is a proof.
Check a friend's puzzle. A child in another class wrote this. Two numbers add up to eight. One number is two more than the other. The numbers are six and two.
Is the puzzle right? How do you know?
No. Six and two make eight, but six is four more than two, not two more. The numbers that fit are five and three. Check every clue.
Before you share a puzzle. One. It has a story, numbers and one question. Two. It has exactly one answer. Three. You checked it a second way. Four. It is your own puzzle, not copied.
Which check would you do first?

If a child writes 6 and 3 for Mi's puzzle and stops, ask: how do you know there is not another pair? If a child says the friend's puzzle is right because 6 and 2 make 8, ask: does the second clue fit? Check every clue.

Key words to use every time: puzzle, rule, check, clue, one answer. The slides keep the answers off the screen while you ask: read every question with its numbers aloud. Class numbers are not used in the workbook.
@rec
Stand up and get a sip of water. We make a quarter turn. We count in threes and clap. Do it with me.

Make a slow quarter turn. Count in threes from nought to eighteen with a clap each time. Ask how many claps to reach eighteen. Then stretch up high and curl small, like a folded shape. Seated children move one arm.
@rec
Pause the recording now, before the Quest starts. Nothing of the Quest is recorded. Then show the Quest slide.

Now it is time for Mi's Challenge Quest! Mi the dolphin is swimming home to the Home Reef after a whole year, and eight gates are in the way. At each gate there is a puzzle for you. You work on your own paper with your quest partner beside you.

It is a game, not a race, and nobody gets a score. Your answers are private: only your grown-up and your tutor may see them. You may skip a gate and Mi will swim round it. I will not say any answers, and I will not show anyone's paper.
Under each gate there is a row of tools. Circle the tool you used. There is no wrong tool. When you have checked your answer, tick I checked.

Children open the closed Quest Log, with a pencil. Quest partners sit beside the child and may talk about how to start, but do not give answers. Paper flat on the table, never held up. Name on page 1. Counters and fingers are fine.

Page 1. Gate 1. Look at the circle. It is folded in half and in half again. Part a: the circle has blank equal parts. Part b: each part is called a blank. Look at the rectangle made of squares. Part c: the rectangle has 3 rows of 3 squares, so blank squares in all. Gate 2. A counter starts at S. It moves only right or up to reach E. Part a: it moves blank steps in all. Part b: there are blank different routes from S to E.

Children work quietly on page 1 (gates 1 and 2); partners may whisper about how, not about the answer. Look around the gallery; say nothing about right or wrong. If asked, re-read a gate to the whole group.
Gates one and two are open! Mi swims on. Turn to page 2.

Gate 3. Look at the stack of cubes. Part a: there are blank cubes in all. Now look at the paper with its dashed fold line, and the paper folded once on that line with one hole punched in it. Part b: when the folded paper is opened there are blank holes. Gate 4. Ben has 5 coins. They are 5-cent coins and 10-cent coins. They make 40 cents. Write how many five-cent coins and how many ten-cent coins.
Children work quietly on page 2 (gates 3 and 4).
Gates three and four are open!
One-minute stretch: stand, shake out your hands, sip some water. Paper stays on the table.
Turn to page 3. The Home Reef is getting closer.

Gate 5. Each line joins two dots. Part a: there are blank lines. Part b: 3 boxes have 5 pencils in each box, so blank pencils in all. Gate 6. Look at the graph. Each picture stands for 2 flowers. Part a: Ali has blank flowers. Part b: Mei has blank more flowers than Ali. Gate 7. A tower has 6 blocks in row 1, 10 blocks in row 2 and 14 blocks in row 3. Each row has 4 more blocks than the row before. Row 5 has blank blocks.
Children work quietly on page 3 (gates 5, 6 and 7).
Gates five, six and seven are open! One gate left. Turn to page 4.

Gate 8. A child in another class wrote a puzzle: I think of a number. I add 5. I get 13. My number is 7. Part a: is the puzzle right? Circle Yes or No. Part b: the right number is blank. The secret cave has one more puzzle, and it is optional. You may skip it. Ali saves 5 cents on Monday, 10 cents on Tuesday and 15 cents on Wednesday. Each day he saves 5 cents more than the day before. Part a: on Friday he saves blank cents. Part b: from Monday to Friday he saves blank cents in all. Then write why you chose your tool.
Children work quietly on page 4: gate 8, then the optional secret cave item if they wish.

You reached the Home Reef! Make sure your name is on every page and close your Quest Log. Well done for a whole year of trying your best. Grown-ups, please take one photo of each page today and send them to the business WhatsApp, as in the note. Mi's tutor will send you one line about what we saw, never a mark.

Say nothing about answers. Remind the group that nothing is added up and no answer is read out. Look back over the year together in a minute (the OUR YEAR card). Restart the recording for the workbook. Children who did not finish may use a few minutes of the workbook time.

A child who says they cannot do a gate: say to the whole group that skipping is fine, Mi swims round it, and they may come back. A child who is upset: the grown-up may stop at any time; do not single the child out. Never give a hint to one child about an answer.

The answers, your private notes sheet for each child, the group advice sheet and the one-line templates for the grown-up are in L40_Quest_Tutor_Notes.pdf. Do not collect or look at any paper during the lesson. Photos arrive only on the program's business WhatsApp and the line goes to the parent only; never a message to a child, and never a personal phone. The exit ticket on workbook page 5 is for home this lesson: the Quest is the exit.
The recording is on again, for the workbook.
@rec

Page 1, Start here. Question 1: look back at your year books. Choose a favourite page, picture or puzzle. Part a: my favourite is blank. Part b: I like it because blank. Many answers are right. Question 2: circle one in each row, I know it well or I am learning it. This is for you and your grown-up. Your tutor only sees it if you choose to share it. Question 3: which one is a clear puzzle? Write its number in the brackets.
Page 1, questions 1 to 3. Tutor walks the cameras, asks how do you know. Wait 10 seconds before helping.
Question 1: many answers are right. Question 2: many answers are right. Question 3: option two. Tick your own page with a tick.

Page 2. Question 4. A child in another class wrote a puzzle and an answer. Siti has nine stickers. Ravi has four more stickers than Siti. How many stickers does Ravi have? The child says five. Part a: is the answer right? Circle Right or Wrong. Part b: the right answer is blank. Question 5. Mi makes a ten first to add nine and seven. Part a: nine and blank make ten. Part b: seven take away your answer to part a is blank. Part c: ten and your answer to part b make blank. Question 6. Under each of questions 4 to 6, write the tool you used and tick I checked. Count by rows. Part a: there are blank rows of dots. Part b: there are blank dots in all.
Page 2, questions 4 to 6.
Question 4: wrong, and thirteen stickers. Question 5: one, then six, then sixteen. Question 6: four rows, and twenty dots. Tick your own page.
Pages three to five are for home this time: a puzzle to write, a puzzle with a proof, and teach it in a minute. Everyone may try them. Nothing is collected.

Q1: flip through your year books and stop at a page you liked. Q2: circle the first one that feels true. Q3: a clear puzzle has a story, numbers and one question. Q4: add, because more means the numbers are joined. Q5: nine needs one more to make ten. Q6: count the dots in one row, then count on by rows.

A child who is still stuck ticks I am still stuck on the look-back page. The grown-up can photograph that page after class and send it to the business WhatsApp (never a personal phone). You then help in the open session when the next program starts. Never a private message to a child.

Think harder has write a puzzle, swap it and solve it, and which puzzle has exactly one answer. Go further has Puzzle With a Proof (beyond Primary 1 on purpose), a friend's puzzle, and writing your own with a proof. Do not announce who is on which page. Start here takes a middle child about 10 minutes, with the tool line. Slow class: take the extra minutes from the flex time and do not skip the answer slides.
@rec
Remember the sneak-peek? Puzzle one: many questions are right, for example, how many pens in all. Puzzle two: no. Four, five, six and seven all fit, so it is not a good puzzle yet.

Now the Showcase. Teach us one idea you found this year, in about a minute. Use the three lines on the slide: my favourite idea is, my tool is and why, here is an example and a check. A pass is always fine.

You may teach your grown-up instead, with your microphone muted, and tell us I taught my grown-up. If you teach us, your voice is recorded. Everyone else listens. Afterwards you may say one thing you learned. There is no voting and no best.
Think time: children choose their idea and say it to their quest partner.
Who would like to teach us an idea? Volunteers first. A pass is always fine.
Thank you. Who would like to teach us the next idea?
Another volunteer. One idea, about a minute.
Thank you. Another idea?
Another volunteer. One idea, about a minute.
Thank you. Is there one more?
Another volunteer, if there is one. One idea, about a minute.
Thank you. One more, if there is one.
Another volunteer, if there is one. One idea, about a minute.
One thing you learned from a friend. You can say it, or you can just nod.
Thank you, inquirers. You found, you tested and you explained, all year.
Optional, no time modelled: ask which tool the group chose and why. Volunteers first; listen for a tool being named and a reason.

Volunteers only, up to five, one at a time; about a minute each. Repeat each idea in your own words for the recording. Never call a child by name to answer; no voting, no best, no ranking, no counting of claps. A child who does not want to be recorded teaches a grown-up with the microphone muted. Puzzles stay inside the group; nothing is collected or compiled; a puzzle leaves the group only if the grown-up agrees. If fewer children volunteer, finish early: the time goes to the flex buffer. Praise the reason, not the speed. A volunteer whose idea has a small mistake: say the right idea in your own words without naming the mistake.
@rec

Pick one problem from today. Did I answer the question? Does my answer make sense? Can I check it another way? Tick, write one word, or pass. If you tick I am still stuck, ask your grown-up to photograph this page after class and send it to our business WhatsApp. Then we will help you.
Children fill in the look-back box on page 5. Nobody reads theirs out. Praise a check you saw, not speed.

Well done, inquirers, for the whole year. What comes next is the first lesson of Level 2 or the holiday program. Your tutor will tell you which one, and the start date. Goodbye, and thank you to the grown-ups.
Optional, only if you are on time. Write a puzzle whose answer is twelve and that has exactly one answer.
Short think time, then take two puzzles from volunteers and check that each has exactly one answer.
Spare-time menu. If the whole class is ahead, pick one or two activities from the guide (about 4 minutes each).

Optional exit ticket. Question 1: Mei thinks of a number. She takes away five and gets nine. What is her number? Question 2: which puzzle has exactly one answer? Option 1: write a number bigger than six. Option 2: I am a number. I am three more than eight. Option 3: Ali has three pens. Option 4: how many pens? Write its number in the bracket. Question 3: a child in another class says seven and eight make sixteen. Circle Right or Wrong.
Children answer E1 to E3 on page 5 on their own.
Question 1: fourteen. Question 2: option two, eleven. Question 3: wrong. Tick your own ticket with a tick.

This is the standing buffer. A child who needs more time for the Quest may use it. If you are behind, finish the look-back and say goodbye. Do not start anything new. Optional slide answer: for example I am a number, I am 5 more than 7. If the whole class is ahead, use the Spare-time menu (guide section 3b) instead of rushing on.

start.text: Look back at your year books. Choose a favourite page, picture or puzzle. Many answers are right.
start.hint: Flip through your books. Stop at a page you liked.
start.solution: Many answers are right. A good answer names the page, picture or puzzle and gives one reason.
mistakes: Writing only that it was fun: add one thing about the maths.
Leaving it blank: you may pass.

start.text: Circle one in each row. This is for you and your grown-up. Your tutor only sees it if you choose to share it.
start.hint: Circle the first one that feels true. You can change it later.
start.solution: Many answers are right. The circles show what to practise: an idea you are learning is a good idea to teach a toy.
mistakes: Ticking one box for every idea without thinking.
Feeling that one box is better: neither box is better.

parts.text: Telling the time on a clock.

start.text: Which one is a clear puzzle? Write its number in the brackets.
start.hint: A clear puzzle has a story, numbers and one question.
start.solution: Option (2) has a story (Ali and Mei), numbers (6 and 3) and one question. Option (1) has no numbers. Option (3) has no question. Option (4) has no story or numbers.
mistakes: Choosing (4), a question with no story.
Choosing (3), a story with no question.

options: Ali has some pens and Mei has some pens.
Ali has 6 pens. Mei has 3 more pens than Ali. How many pens does Mei have?
Ali has 6 pens. Mei has 3 more pens.
How many pens does Mei have?

start.text: A child in another class wrote a puzzle and an answer. Siti has 9 stickers. Ravi has 4 more stickers than Siti. How many stickers does Ravi have? The child says 5.
start.hint: More means we join the numbers. Do we add or take away?
start.solution: Ravi has 4 more than 9, so 9 + 4 = 13 stickers. The answer 5 is 9 take away 4, which is not what 4 more means. Check: 13 take away 9 is 4.
mistakes: Saying Right because 9 and 4 are in the puzzle.

parts.text: Is the answer right? Circle Right or Wrong.

parts.ans: Any tool that fits. A reason matters more than the name.

start.text: Mi makes a ten first to add 9 + 7. Fill in the blanks.
start.hint: 9 needs 1 more to make 10. Take that 1 from the 7.
start.solution: 9 and 1 make 10. 7 take away 1 is 6. 10 and 6 make 16.
mistakes: Forgetting to take the 1 from the 7.

parts.text: 7 take away your answer to part a is [] .
10 and your answer to part b make [] .

parts.ans: Any tool that fits. A reason matters more than the name.

start.text: Count by rows. Look at the apples.
start.hint: Count the apples in one row. Then count on by rows.
start.solution: There are 4 rows of 5 apples: 5, 10, 15, 20. There are 20 apples in all.
mistakes: Writing the apples in one row only.

parts.ans: Any tool that fits. A reason matters more than the name.

think.text: Write a puzzle for a new Level 1 child. It needs a story, numbers, one question and one answer. Use two numbers up to 20. Many answers are right.
think.hint: Start with two numbers and a name. Then write one question.
think.solution: Many answers are right. A good puzzle has a story, numbers, one question and exactly one answer, for example: Wei has 8 stickers. Lily has 5 more stickers than Wei. How many stickers does Lily have? The answer is 13.
mistakes: Writing a story with no question.
Writing a puzzle with two answers.

think.text: Read your puzzle from question T1 to your quest partner. Your partner solves it. Fill in the blanks.
think.hint: Read your puzzle slowly. Do not say your answer.
think.solution: Many answers are right. If your partner gets a different answer, your puzzle may have two answers or a mistake. Check it again.
mistakes: Telling your partner the answer first.

parts.text: Is it the same as mine? Circle Yes or No.

think.text: Puzzle A: Write a number bigger than 10 and smaller than 15. Puzzle B: I am a number. I am 4 more than 9. Puzzle C: Ali has 3 pens and Mei has 4 pens.
think.hint: A puzzle with one answer has only one number that fits.
think.solution: Puzzle B has exactly one answer: 13. Puzzle A has four answers: 11, 12, 13 and 14. Puzzle C has no question.
mistakes: Choosing C (it has numbers but no question).
Writing 5 for puzzle A (11 to 15 counted).

parts.text: Which puzzle has exactly one answer? Circle A, B or C.

go.text: Mi's puzzle: Two jars hold 12 shells in all. The blue jar holds 4 more shells than the red jar. Fill in the table of every pair that makes 12. Then answer (a) and (b).
go.hint: Start at 0 and 12. Take 1 from the blue jar and give it to the red jar. Find the difference each time.
go.solution: The pairs are 0 and 12, 1 and 11, 2 and 10, 3 and 9, 4 and 8, 5 and 7, 6 and 6. The differences are 12, 10, 8, 6, 4, 2 and 0. Only 4 and 8 differ by 4. So the red jar holds 4 and the blue jar holds 8, and no other pair works.
mistakes: Stopping at 4 and 8 without listing every pair.

parts.text: The red jar holds [] shells and the blue jar holds [] shells.

go.text: A child in another class wrote a puzzle: Two numbers add up to 10. One number is 4 more than the other. The numbers are 6 and 4.
go.hint: Check each clue. Do 6 and 4 add up to 10? Is 6 four more than 4?
go.solution: 6 + 4 = 10, so the first clue fits. 6 take away 4 is 2, not 4, so the second clue does not fit. The numbers that fit are 3 and 7: 3 + 7 = 10 and 7 take away 3 is 4.
mistakes: Saying Yes because the numbers add up to 10.

parts.text: Is the puzzle right? Circle Yes or No.
The numbers that fit are [] and [] .

go.text: Write a puzzle with a rule for a friend. Solve it. Then show why your answer must be right: draw it, list every case, or check a second way. Many answers are right.
go.hint: Use two numbers. Make a rule. Try every case, like the table in G1.
go.solution: Many answers are right. A good puzzle has a rule, one answer, and a proof: every case is listed, or the answer is checked a second way. For example: Two numbers add up to 8. One is 2 more than the other. 0 and 8, 1 and 7, 2 and 6, 3 and 5, 4 and 4. Only 3 and 5 are 2 apart.
mistakes: Writing a puzzle with two answers.
Copying a puzzle from a book or from class.

investigation.title: Teach it in a minute
investigation.first: Write the name of your favourite idea from the year: ____
investigation.text: Write or draw how you will teach it: the idea, one example and one check. Then teach it to your grown-up.
investigation.answer: Many answers are right. A good plan names the idea, gives an example with numbers or a picture, and one check.
investigation.look_for: A child who names an idea from the year, gives one example with numbers or a picture, and says one check. Credit any clear idea. A child who writes only the name has the first step: ask, what is an example? A child who chooses an idea from the last lessons has looked back well; one from Term 1 has too.
mistakes: Naming an idea but giving no example.
Teaching a puzzle that has two answers.

talk.question: Teach us one favourite idea from the year in about a minute. Use the frame: My favourite idea is ___. It works like this: ___. Here is an example: ___. Everyone else listens.
talk.answer: Many answers are right. A model: My favourite idea is make a ten. It works like this: to add 9 + 4, take 1 from the 4 to make 10, then add the 3 that is left. Here is an example: 9 + 4 = 10 + 3 = 13.
talk.look_for: A child who names an idea, says how it works and gives an example. A pass is always fine, and a child may teach a grown-up instead. Never compare ideas and never say best.

exit.text: Mei thinks of a number. She takes away 5 and gets 9.
exit.solution: Work backwards: 9 and 5 make 14. Check: 14 take away 5 is 9.

exit.text: Which puzzle has exactly one answer? Write its number in the bracket.
exit.solution: Option (2) has one answer: 3 more than 8 is 11. Option (1) has many answers. Option (3) has no question. Option (4) has no story.
mistakes: Choosing (1): many numbers are bigger than 6.

options: I am a number. I am 3 more than 8.

exit.text: A child in another class says 7 + 8 = 16.
exit.solution: 7 + 8 = 15, not 16. Check: 16 take away 8 is 8, not 7.

home_practice.text: A puzzle says: I am a number. I am 5 more than 12. What number am I? ___
home_practice.solution: 12 and 5 make 17. Check: 17 take away 12 is 5.

home_practice.text: Two numbers add up to 14. One number is 2 more than the other. The numbers are ___ and ___ .
home_practice.solution: List the pairs: 6 and 8 add up to 14, and 8 is 2 more than 6. Check: no other pair that adds up to 14 is 2 apart.

home_practice.text: A child in another class says 20 take away 8 is 13. Circle Right or Wrong: ___ . The right answer is ___ .
home_practice.solution: 20 take away 8 is 12. Check: 12 and 8 make 20.

home_practice.text: Write a number bigger than 7 and smaller than 12. How many numbers fit this puzzle? ___ numbers.
home_practice.solution: 8, 9, 10 and 11 all fit, so there are 4 numbers. A good puzzle has exactly one answer, so this one needs another clue.

home_practice.text: 5 pens cost $10. How much does 1 pen cost? $___
home_practice.solution: $10 shared equally among 5 pens is $2 each.

slips.say: That is 11 take away 4. More means we add.

items.hint: List the pairs that make 16. Find the pair that is 6 apart.
steps: The pairs are 5 and 11, 4 and 12, and so on.
5 and 11 make 16, and 11 is 6 more than 5.

tpl.hint: List the pairs that make {t}. Find the pair that is {d} apart.
steps: Find the pair that is {d} apart.

items.q: Which one is a good puzzle?

steps: A good puzzle has a story, numbers and one question.
The second one has all three.
items.answer: Ali has 5 pens. Mei has 3 more pens than Ali. How many pens does Mei have?

a: How many pens does Mei have?
slips.say: That is only a question. A good puzzle has a story and numbers too.

options: Ali has 5 pens. Mei has 3 more pens than Ali. How many pens does Mei have?
How many pens does Mei have?

beyond.name: Puzzle With a Proof
beyond.text: Two jars hold 12 shells and the blue jar holds 4 more than the red jar: list every pair that makes 12 (0 and 12 up to 6 and 6), find the differences, and see that only 4 and 8 differ by 4. questions.skill: Halves and quarters of a circle, and a rectangle made of squares (Term 4 Lessons 1 and 2)
questions.text: A circle is folded in half and in half again. A rectangle is made of 3 rows of 3 squares.

parts.text: The rectangle has ___ squares in all.

questions.say: Gate 1. Look at the circle. It is folded in half and in half again. Part a: the circle has blank equal parts. Part b: each part is called a blank. Look at the rectangle made of squares. Part c: the rectangle has 3 rows of 3 squares, so blank squares in all.
questions.solution: Half and half again makes 4 equal parts, and each part is a quarter. 3 rows of 3 squares: 3, 6, 9 squares.

questions.skill: Steps and routes on a dot grid (Term 4 Lesson 3)
questions.text: A counter starts at S. It moves only right or up to reach E.

parts.text: There are ___ different routes from S to E.

questions.say: Gate 2. A counter starts at S. It moves only right or up to reach E. Part a: it moves blank steps in all. Part b: there are blank different routes from S to E.
questions.solution: 2 steps right and 1 step up make 3 steps. The routes are right right up, right up right, and up right right: 3 routes.

questions.skill: Cubes in a stack, and a paper folded once and punched once (Term 4 Lesson 4)
questions.text: Look at the stack of cubes. Then look at the paper with its dashed fold line, and the folded paper with one hole.

parts.text: The paper is folded once on the dashed line and one hole is punched. When it is opened there are ___ holes.

questions.say: Gate 3. Look at the stack of cubes. Part a: there are blank cubes in all. Now look at the paper with its dashed fold line, and the paper folded once on that line with one hole punched in it. Part b: when the folded paper is opened there are blank holes.
questions.solution: The stacks have 2, 2, 1 and 1 cubes: 2 and 2 make 4, and 1 and 1 more make 6 cubes. A folded paper has 2 layers, so one hole goes through both: 2 holes.

questions.skill: Five coins that make an amount (mixed: no lesson tag)
questions.text: Ben has 5 coins. They are 5-cent coins and 10-cent coins. They make 40 cents.

parts.text: Ben has ___ five-cent coins and ___ ten-cent coins.

questions.say: Gate 4. Ben has 5 coins. They are 5-cent coins and 10-cent coins. They make 40 cents. Write how many five-cent coins and how many ten-cent coins.
questions.solution: Try 3 and 2: 15 and 20 make 35, too low. Try 2 and 3: 10 and 30 make 40. That is 5 coins.

questions.skill: Counting lines and equal groups (Term 4 Lesson 6)
questions.text: Each line joins two dots. 3 boxes have 5 pencils in each box.

parts.text: The 3 boxes have ___ pencils in all.

questions.say: Gate 5. Each line joins two dots. Part a: there are blank lines. Part b: 3 boxes have 5 pencils in each box, so blank pencils in all.
questions.solution: Count each line once: 5 lines round the edge and 2 lines inside make 7 lines. 3 boxes of 5 pencils: 5, 10, 15 pencils.
mistakes: (a) 5 (the lines inside missed) or 8 (a line counted twice).

questions.skill: Reading a picture graph with each picture standing for 2 (Term 4 Lessons 7 and 8)
questions.text: Look at the graph. Each picture stands for 2 flowers.

parts.text: Mei has ___ more flowers than Ali.

questions.say: Gate 6. Look at the graph. Each picture stands for 2 flowers. Part a: Ali has blank flowers. Part b: Mei has blank more flowers than Ali.
questions.solution: Ali has 4 pictures: 2, 4, 6, 8 flowers. Mei has 7 pictures, which is 3 more pictures than Ali, and 3 pictures of 2 are 6 more flowers.

questions.skill: A growing tower (mixed: no lesson tag)
questions.text: A tower has 6 blocks in row 1, 10 blocks in row 2 and 14 blocks in row 3. Each row has 4 more blocks than the row before.
questions.say: Gate 7. A tower has 6 blocks in row 1, 10 blocks in row 2 and 14 blocks in row 3. Each row has 4 more blocks than the row before. Row 5 has blank blocks.
questions.solution: Add 4 each time: 6, 10, 14, 18, 22. Row 5 has 22 blocks.

questions.text: A child in another class wrote a puzzle: I think of a number. I add 5. I get 13. My number is 7.

parts.text: Is the puzzle right? Circle Yes or No. [yesno]

questions.say: Gate 8. A child in another class wrote a puzzle: I think of a number. I add 5. I get 13. My number is 7. Part a: is the puzzle right? Circle Yes or No. Part b: the right number is blank.
questions.solution: Check: 7 and 5 make 12, not 13. Work backwards: 13 take away 5 is 8. Check: 8 and 5 make 13.

optional.skill: Bus fare going up 10 cents a day (money in cents and a growing pattern joined)
optional.text: Think harder (optional). Mi's bus ride costs 20¢ on Day 1, 30¢ on Day 2 and 40¢ on Day 3. Each day it costs 10¢ more than the day before.
optional.say: The secret cave has one more puzzle, and it is optional. You may skip it. Mi's bus ride costs 20 cents on Day 1, 30 cents on Day 2 and 40 cents on Day 3. Each day it costs 10 cents more than the day before. Part a: on Day 5 it costs blank cents. Part b: it costs 80 cents on Day blank.
optional.solution: Day 1 20, Day 2 30, Day 3 40, Day 4 50, Day 5 60, Day 6 70, Day 7 80. So Day 5 costs 60 cents and 80 cents is Day 7.

parent_note.title: Mi's Challenge Quest: a note for grown-ups
parent_note.what: In the last lesson of the year we play Mi's Challenge Quest. Mi the dolphin swims home to the Home Reef and meets 8 gates, each with a short puzzle, plus an optional secret cave. It takes about 20 minutes, straight after the break. Your child works on private paper with you (or a brother or sister) as quest partner. It is a game: nothing is added up, there is no league table and nobody is compared with anyone else. It helps us see what each child enjoyed and what to practise next. The gates look back over Term 4: shapes, grids, cubes, spotting, counting, a picture graph, choosing a tool and checking a puzzle. Every gate is at Start here level, in fresh numbers, except the picture graph where each picture stands for 2 (taught in Term 4 Lesson 8).
before: The Quest Log (4 pages) is in your child's Term 4 book (Book 8). Keep those 4 pages closed until the tutor says to open them. If your book has not arrived or is damaged, message us on WhatsApp within 7 days and we will send you the PDF straight away.
We send you this note a week before the lesson.
Have a pencil, a rubber and a quiet table. Counters and fingers are fine.
during: Be the quest partner: sit beside your child. You may talk about how to start and ask 'how do you know?', but please do not give answers or hints.
Skipping a gate is fine; Mi swims round it. If your child is upset, you may stop at any time.
The paper stays flat on the table. Cameras may be on or off.
after: The same day, take ONE clear photo of each of the 4 pages: page flat, straight from above, the whole page in view. Make sure your child's name is on each page.
Send the photos to the program's business WhatsApp, +65 9880 5962. Please send them to this number only: not to a tutor's own phone, not to the class chat, and never through a child.

We use the photos only to write one line about your child. WhatsApp is a messaging service run by another company. We keep the photos for 90 days after the program ends, then delete them, as our privacy notice says.
parent_note.back: Within a few days we send you ONE line, written from our private notes, about what we saw your child do in the Quest, with a small next step if it helps. It only describes what your child did, and it never compares children. If you would rather not play the Quest, tell us: that is fine.
